item.description: ⚽️ Head coach departs after one win in 11 games ⚽️ Carrick sacked with Pochettino poised to take over ⚽️ Have any thoughts? Email Luke “ After going through the Moyes season ,” writes Hugh, “the dross football of Mourinho and Van Gaal, the moments-years of Solskjaer, the Rangnick surgery that never was, the middling Ten Hag, the baffling Amorim, and now a decent man thrust into the meat grinder, this is the first year it’s been genuinely hard to watch Man Utd with any emotion. “And it’s not because of the football. It’s that the Glazer ownership and Ratcliffe mismanagement has met the Man City revelations, meaning it’s hard to see the point anymore. £1bn taken out of the club while others were illicitly pumping in roughly the same. A club drained of life, hollowed out … I can take crap football, but I can’t take this anymore.” Continue reading...

(See 10.35am .) Commenting on the proposals, revealed by Milburn in an interview in the Times, Siân Berry , the Green MP and the party’s work and pensions spokesperson, said: So the solution to young people without education or jobs is to continue demonising young and disabled people instead of addressing the structural inequalities stacked against them? What is the point of a deep review like this if the conclusion is that the government goes on blaming young people for needing help? The waiting list for hospital treatment has also risen to its highest level in nearly a year. item.title: Billions lost and markets roiled by one man’s indiscretion. Isn’t it now clear that these tech bros are too powerful? | Aditya Chakrabortty
item.description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair must be the costliest fling in human history – and a preview of what awaits when the tech bubble bursts One thing we all know about the tech billionaires is they are super-smart. We know this largely because they never stop telling us. The “ cognitive elite ”, to use their favoured phrase, are entitled to shape our future without our say-so. When Elon Musk goes hiring, he wants “super-high-IQ small-government revolutionaries”. Long before they got private jets, what fuelled these boys was faith in their own brainpower. As a teenager, Jensen Huang wooed his future wife, Lori, thus: “If you do homework with me every Sunday, I promise you you’ll get straight As.” Lord Byron: I believe it’s your move. Continue reading...

item.title: Victorian Psycho review – Maika Monroe has a blast in unsteady horror romp
item.description: The It Follows and Longlegs star tears into the role of a murderous governess in this hit-and-miss adaptation of Virginia Feito’s gory novel It’s not that hard to figure out why a lower-class woman toiling away in Victorian England would be so easily driven to violently murder everyone around her. If it’s not the brittle entitlement of those who employ you, it’s the unending misogyny of the system you’re forced to be a subservient part of, all the while being underpaid and undervalued and at the mercy of sexual violence, a multitude of diseases and an average lifespan of just 42. As Winifred Notty (Maika Monroe) fills the frame in Victorian Psycho, heading to a new job as governess for a rich family, it’s easy to be on her side. Even as her murderous impulses start to rear their head, they’re made somewhat understandable, although Winifred isn’t just a woman reacting to the various injustices of the time – she’s one responding to a demon within her, a darkness she has chosen to embrace

item.title: NHS England deletes ‘misleading’ claim 137 trusts benefiting from Palantir AI tools
item.description: Exclusive: The Guardian revealed 29 hospital trusts were not or hardly using the controversial patient data tech NHS England has deleted a claim from its website stating 137 hospital trusts are benefiting from Palantir’s AI health data system after the Guardian revealed 29 of them were not using all or most of the controversial technology. Health bosses had published a list of all the NHS bodies “live” with and “realising benefits” from the AI-powered federated data platform (FDP), a system set up to improve patient outcomes, boost operating theatre efficiency and speed up bed discharges. But after 29 trusts said it was either not live or they were not using any of its applications, the original list of hospitals appears to have been taken down. Continue reading...

item.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
item.description: Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others? How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation. The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly

item.title: First guidelines on attempts to manipulate the ocean put spotlight on geoengineering industry
item.description: Proponents argue ocean carbon removal is necessary to counteract the effects of the climate crisis but critics say more research is needed A cluster of candy cane-striped smoke stacks dots the horizon of Tufts Cove in Nova Scotia, Canada. Deep in the briny depths of Halifax harbour, something huge is happening: the ocean is being engineered to remove atmospheric carbon. “This is what Mother Nature has done naturally for a few billion years in order to rebalance the atmospheric and ocean chemistry over long timescales,” says Dr Greg Rau, co-founder and senior scientist at Planetary Technologies. Continue reading...

item.title: Datacentres are deeply unpopular. Has Sweden made one we can all love?
item.description: It is built of wood, resembles an Ikea and its power is totally renewable. Plus, it was built with the local community in mind. Is this facility in Falun the best datacentre in the world? ‘It was pretty cool, when they were building it. It looked like a very large Ikea,” says John Wernvik, of EcoDataCenter. He is giving me a tour of their facility in Falun, Sweden, which could lay claim to being the world’s greenest datacentre – although to many, that is a contradiction in terms. One difference is immediately visible: this datacentre is made out of wood. Huge panels of cross-laminated timber arrived at the site pre-cut, and were assembled by crane according to instructions, like flatpack furniture. Aesthetically, this section of the datacentre is more like an Ikea before the fit-out, a cavernous, echoey, immaculately clean hangar. The wood is not EcoDataCenter’s only claim to sustainability; it is more than just cosmetic, says Wernvik, the company’s chief external relations and sustain

item.title: ‘Maga is dead, Maga is effeminate’: why has the manosphere rejected Trump?
item.description: As public mood has shifted on Israel-Gaza and the Iran war, so has the manosphere’s devotion to the US president Earlier this week, Donald Trump announced that the UFC president, Dana White, was to become his press secretary. The US president hoped the creator of Power Slap, a face-slapping league which one of the world’s leading neurologists called “a sport inconsistent with the intelligence of humans”, might be the right man to deliver his daily rebuttals to the media. Trump later backtracked on the appointment, saying he was “only kidding” , yet it is easy to understand why he might be pining for White’s muscles, trash talk and thirst for athletic violence. White is representative of the way Trump transcended politics in 2024 to become a celebrated figure in the manosphere, the loosely defined cluster of male content creators who have a direct line to America’s bored and aggrieved young men. On the night of the 2024 election, White stood at the victory podium reading out “thank yous

item.title: Pete Hegseth’s wake of destruction at the Pentagon – Stateside with Kai and Carter
item.description: Pete Hegseth has managed to dodge an impeachment trial, for the second time. And Republicans have avoided — for now — a major public accounting of the damage done at the Pentagon during Hegseth’s tenure. Thomas Massie’s articles of impeachment detail charges that are likely to return when Democrats take the majority next year. Kai Wright speaks with Guardian senior political enterprise reporter Aram Roston about how people inside the military have reacted to the impeachment and to Hegseth’s tenure, from the boat strikes in the Caribbean to the massive loss of experienced leadership and a dramatic depletion of munitions in Iran. Roston, who has covered the Pentagon across several administrations, describes a Pentagon shaken up in ways he’s never before seen. Continue reading...

item.title: Trump ran on a platform of peace. His war may have cost Republicans the midterms | Mohamad Bazzi
item.description: Voters remembered Trump’s many promises to avoid the same kind of regime-change wars started by his predecessors For much of his political career, Donald Trump ranted at past US presidents who got the US entangled in endless foreign conflicts. He used it as a cudgel to belittle his predecessors, calling George W Bush’s decision to invade Iraq in 2003 “the worst single mistake ever made in the history of our country”. Trump also regularly derided the occupation of Afghanistan as “a total disaster”. Then Trump decided to launch his own disastrous war against Iran eight months ago. Tasked with repairing an ancient shrine in the weeks leading up to a local festival, you’ll find yourself cleaning out trash, mending broken arches and slowly bringing a small rural community back together. It sounds a bit like JL Carr’s compact but enchanting novel A Month in the Country , except instead of shell-shocked veterans of the first world war you’re left exploring the rich inner life of a Japanese racoon dog who can ride a BMX. I forget its exact name – something like WXYZ Tradify or Crypto Max 301 or Wealth Centaur would be my guess. But I remember there was a mind-shreddingly banal male voiceover (“diversify your forex contingents and start making your money bleed today”), to which England players like Harry Brook and Jacob Bethell were depicted engaging in various feats of staged cricketing heroism. Right up until the moment Shoaib Bashir steps up to bowl. Bashir delivers his trademark off-break with that famously high release point. Kane will draw level with players including Dani Alves, Eden Hazard and Paolo Maldini on 126 caps. Illustrious players, none of whom lead their country’s appearance standings. item.title: The Booker prize winner described a dystopian Britain. But haven’t we been living in that since Brexit? | Zoe Williams
item.description: It didn’t need a novel: even Leave voters understand the damage that has been done, as does the PM. Now all he has to do is persuade his party Earlier this week, some people on the radio were talking about a very British dystopia. The government had disintegrated, but everyone was carrying on pretty much as they had before. Britain was isolated on the world stage and people missed Europe like hell, but weren’t allowed to visit, let alone live there. I thought the radio people were discussing Britain post-Brexit, circa 2022. In fact, they were talking about the plot of the Booker prize-winning novel The End of Everything . Its author, M John Harrison, is renowned now for being, at 81, the oldest winner of the award, as well as the first science fiction writer to win it. But let’s also carve out a space for him on the podium of dystopian fiction, as a writer who can describe an indeterminate future in terms that are both terrifying and sound like a couple of years ago. item.title: ‘I railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian’: the cheeky, feminist photography of Jill Posener
item.description: Her witty photos served as a rebuttal to 80s misogyny and Thatcherite conservatism. Now 50 years on, the photographer is receiving an overdue retrospective. ‘I loved that we could respond with humour,’ she says. If it were a lady it would get its bottom pinched. If this lady was a car she’d run you down.” These are the words that Jill Posener immortalised in November 1979, when she picked her way through traffic on London’s Farringdon Road to photograph something most would have overlooked: a graffitied billboard. The first sentence was there by design – a sexist attempt at wit intended to promote a new Fiat. The second she has since been repeatedly accused of adding herself. In reality, the image-maker, playwright and nonprofit founder explains from her home in California, the now infamous phrase had been daubed by two women working at the nearby offices of the socialist newspaper Morning Star. “They had seen the billboard go up and were so incensed that they came up with this solutio

item.title: Russia's 'hidden mobilization': The 'expendable' lives fueling Putin's war on Ukraine
item.description: Erin Ogunkeye is pleased to welcome John Lough, Senior Research Fellow and Head of Foreign Policy & International Partnerships at the New Eurasian Strategies Centre (NEST Centre), He is also an Associate Fellow with the Russia & Eurasia Programme at Chatham House. Lough offers a sobering assessment of the social and strategic dynamics sustaining Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He argues that the Kremlin has disproportionately recruited soldiers from poorer and politically marginalised communities, including ethnic minority regions, where the human cost of the conflict is less likely to generate organised opposition. Many of those recruited, he explains, "have been recruited for a deliberate reason because they were seen, you know, ultimately as lives that were expendable, in other words as cannon fodder."

item.title: Allen review – what would happen if ET came back for Elliott as an adult? Turns out nothing great
item.description: This good-natured if relentlessly unsubtle family film from Netflix and the studio behind Bluey relies on a cute alien with no personality It’s important for stories about magical formative experiences to make the point that time marches forward. Puff the Magic Dragon slinks back into his cave; Max bids farewell to the Wild Things and returns home; the snowman melts, leaving behind only a hat and scarf. It’s not just about the passage of time, but the melancholic act of saying goodbye – the child moving on, the experience imprinted on to their psyches. Allen, the first live-action feature from Ludo Studio – the production company behind a little show called Bluey – has a quirky point of difference. Instead of following a child who befriends a cute little alien then grows into a man enriched by the brief relationship, that child becomes a manchild – unable to move on and haunted by the feeling that his best days are behind him. This twist on convention is enough to pique our interest, b

Here the main character is Bethany Peters, a young trans woman working as a content moderator at a YouTube-like company called GlobalVill. Her job is to watch “offensive, illegal, disturbing videos that have no place on the internet” and press a red button to remove those that violate the code of conduct. item.title: ‘A web of canals and cobbled streets’: a city break in Haarlem in the Netherlands
item.description: A short ride from Amsterdam, this laid-back city has great museums, cosy bars and a new exhibition featuring the works of Rembrandt and local artist Frans Hals this winter It’s only 15 minutes away from the Dutch capital by train, but Haarlem feels a million miles from Amsterdam, and perhaps provides a more typical glimpse of the Netherlands than trailing around the well-worn tourist trail of Van Gogh, coffee shops and red lights. An attractive city of cobbled streets, gabled houses and canals, Haarlem is, as the Dutch would say, a gezellig sort of place – cosy, convivial, and full of intriguing nooks and corners. I’ve been coming here for years, and it seems odd that Haarlem is not better known, at least to UK visitors. This winter there’s the added draw of an exhibition devoted to the works of a local boy, the 17th-century painter Frans Hals, and his better-known contemporary Rembrandt in the city’s Frans Hals Museum (until 28 February 2027). item.title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
item.description: In today’s newsletter: US intelligence reportedly believes the former tech executive was recruited by Beijing, raising questions about the security of the AI industry and Trump’s close ties to Nvidia chief Jensen Huang Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies. Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines. item.description: The unofficial Taliban restriction has forced women into desperate and absurd situations as they seek medical help, according to interviews given to the Guardian and Zan Times Farida*, 37, woke up in excruciating pain one night with a toothache. Over the next few days, the pain intensified. “My teeth had been ruined for years. My molars on both sides of my mouth were severely damaged. I couldn’t sleep at night and could barely eat.” Farida and her family had returned from Iran earlier this year to live in Herat, a city in western Afghanistan. item.description: Selahattin Demirtaş lit up the Turkish left in 2014, but was imprisoned for ‘terrorist propaganda’. A tall, talented, human rights lawyer then still in his 30s, a founder of Amnesty’s Diyarbakır branch in eastern Turkey , he was adept at thinking on his feet. And could he talk. His witty satirical speeches , broadcast on the evening news, annoyed Turkey’s establishment politicians on the right and left alike. Demirtaş’s meteoric rise began in 2010, when he became the chair of Turkey’s main pro-Kurdish party, the Peace and Democracy party (BDP). I voted for Demirtaş in the 2014 presidential election , when he was 41. Despite his loss to Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Demirtaş’s 9.7% vote share cheered up leftists such as me on what promised to be another sad election night. item.title: Bronze leg found in Scottish bog sheds new light on Roman occupation
item.description: Once thought to have been looted by Scottish tribes, the gilded limb is the centrepiece of a new exhibition on Roman Scotland in Edinburgh A large bronze leg found in a bog in rural Scotland more than 200 years ago and then hidden away in a duke’s storeroom is helping to rewrite the history of the Roman empire. Antiquarians argued that the so-called Milsington leg had been looted, perhaps from York, hacked off by marauding Scottish tribes and carried north over Hadrian’s Wall. “We cannot visualise the conditions which would have led to its erection anywhere north of the Great Wall,” said one scholar, James Curle, in 1932. item.description: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book. His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse . item.title: Prima Facie review – Cynthia Erivo’s brilliant barrister blazes in sexual assault drama
item.description: Adaptation of the international stage hit stars a commanding Erivo as Tessa, whose career defending rape suspects is undermined by experience A blazingly fierce, effortlessly commanding central performance from Cynthia Erivo, like something from classical drama, powers this movie adaptation of Suzie Miller’s international stage hit (which starred Sheridan Harbridge in the original Australian production , and then Jodie Comer in London’s West End ). Miller has written the screenplay, with Susanna White directing . In the theatre, it is a bravura solo spectacle, a stream-of-consciousness torrent which puts you right inside the trauma and the terror. The movie opens things out to a more conventionally presented drama and we lose something of that overwhelming moment-by-moment access to the lead character’s inner thoughts. But the resulting story is robustly constructed and tremendously acted. Continue reading...

item.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis

The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. item.title: Bird flu has caused catastrophic die-offs – could a wave of extinctions follow?
item.description: As the IUCN global conservation body prepares to update its red list of endangered species, scientists explain why calculating the true toll of a pandemic is so hard It began with the brown skuas. The migratory seabirds had arrived on the sub-Antarctic island of South Georgia in 2023, harbouring a deadly passenger. Within months, the southern elephant seals that had come ashore to breed became sick. Mothers and newborn pups were weak and trembling, with many struggling to breathe. What followed was a horrific mass casualty event, caused by the highly infectious avian influenza (H5N1). By 2025, more than 53,000 female elephant seals had died on South Georgia. Like his idol Jorge Luis Borges, Gospodinov tends towards subversion in his fiction: he takes the “game” and rewrites the rules, turns the board upside down to find new ways of looking and seeing. If the ending is a foregone conclusion, Gospodinov’s magic is to make his stories feel like beginnings with endless possibilities. Yes, it can be revealed, Kane loved to reward himself after a gruelling 90 minutes with a bag of sweets. “I do like a Haribo,” he said with a smile after the Nations League win against Czechia in Prague at the end of September. item.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03409-0 As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

item.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

item.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11232-w Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

item.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

item.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

item.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

item.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7 IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

item.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

item.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11259-z The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

item.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

item.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11280-2 Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

item.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

item.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11240-w A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

item.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2 Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

item.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11191-2 A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

item.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

item.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4 A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

item.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0 Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.

item.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11265-1 Severe drought and warming will substantially increase the loss of suitable climatic area for cactus species.

item.title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11272-2 A transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric enables high-quality interfaces with two-dimensional semiconductors, yielding near-ideal switching, low hysteresis and ultra-low-power complementary transistors and inverters.

item.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9 An imaging algorithm using closure-invariant formalism and diffusion-based reconstruction applied to supermassive black hole very long baseline radio interferometry datasets enables independent recovery of the ring-like shadow and mass that is free from the usual calibration and imaging assumptions.

item.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11249-1 Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: Metasurface waveguides for all-day augmented reality glasses
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11277-x An all-day-wearable augmented reality glasses prototype using a dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide and three matched grating patterns achieves a 30° field of view in an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional eyebox while maintaining high luminance efficiency.

item.title: What happens to your brain when the days get darker? - video
item.description: As the nights draw in, many of us can experience low mood. But for a small proportion of people a more intense depression develops through the winter months. It’s a phenomenon that since the 1980s has been labelled seasonal affective disorder, or Sad, and can be debilitating for sufferers. To find out more about the latest scientific understanding of Sad, Ian Sample speaks to Russell Foster, professor of circadian neuroscience at the University of Oxford. He explains what scientists think the mechanism for the condition could be and what the evidence says about the best way to tackle it. In the UK and Ireland, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org . item.title: From W-M to the No 10, shirt numbers tell a story of football’s tactical evolution
item.description: In the days before squad numbers, the number on a shirt was an indicator of position, as well as the attributes a player was supposed to demonstrate Ultimate 1-50: check out our complete list of players Numbers have a fascination. The No 10 is revered almost everywhere, but perhaps most especially in Argentina, where it denotes the playmaker, the enganche , the quasi-mythical figure who links the front and back of the team. Liverpool and Manchester United have reasons to celebrate their No 7. Ajax retired No 14 for Johan Cruyff, Milan their No 3 and No 6 for Paolo Maldini and Franco Baresi respectively and Birmingham their 22 for Jude Bellingham as gestures of respect for their abilities. Other numbers have been retired to mark premature deaths: the No 20 at Liverpool for Diogo Jota, the No 23 at Manchester City for Marc-Vivian Foé, the 21 at Espanyol for Daniel Jarque. item.title: The laundry miracle: how to solve 10 stubborn problems – from stains to rough towels to ‘permastank’
item.description: For 1 million people on Reddit, the science of clothes-washing is a regular topic of discussion. I tried out their tips and discovered some simple, sustainable answers It started with a sunscreen stain – a yellowed collar on a white T-shirt that persisted wash after wash. A spray of stain remover did nothing; drying the shirt in the sun made it worse. An internet rabbit hole took me to the r/laundry subreddit , where I found my people: 995,000 of them, nerding out over the chemistry of clothes-washing. “People want to take better care of their stuff, but don’t have the knowledge,” says Eric Thompson, a former management consultant based near Seattle who moderates the forum under the name KismaiAesthetics. He took on the mantle after seeing someone suggest white vinegar to treat a burrito stain on an anorak. “If you pour vinegar on a burrito grease stain on white nylon, you now have orange nylon for eternity,” he says. “Acids bind colour to dye sites on nylon.” Continue reading...

item.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
item.description: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely. Surprisingly, Mars may have had a better chance of receiving these cosmic ingredients, although even there the odds were slim. The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.

item.title: Football Daily | Manchester United, Aston Villa and the unseriousness of a 4-4 draw
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Precisely 13,266 games have been played since the inception of the Premier League, and 19 of those matches have finished 4-4 (0.1%), a rarity in a division dominated by the mighty 1-0 (17.6%). It was about time we got one, though. The months of August and September, when teams are still fighting to define their top-flight seasons and fitness and motivation tend to be at their peak, have never seen a single 4-4 draw. As motivation decreases the chances of stupid scorelines increase, and that’s where the 4-4 creeps in. There’s a certain on-the-beachness inherent in the score, and it is no coincidence that it has occurred more in the second half of April, as thoughts drift to the close season and the ineffable pointlessness of a lot of late-campaign football becomes unavoidable, than in the entirety of any other month. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. item.title: Apple pushing faster on agentic Siri would carry three big risks
item.description: Yesterday saw two reports about Apple software development. item.title: U2: Carnaval de Luz review – rousing, restorative rock from a band ready to take on the world again
item.description: (Island) On their first album of new songs in nearly a decade, even earnest Bono-isms carry weight amid music that is impassioned and rejuvenated Even artists who enjoy a seemingly unstoppable imperial period eventually seem to encounter spells of turbulence when the creative planets no longer align – which has been the story of U2’s last 20 years. Try as they might, nothing has matched their earlier albums – especially that mostly uninterrupted golden run from their 1980 debut Boy to 90s benchmarks Achtung Baby and Zooropa. They’ve tried going more pop, becoming more experimental, touring 1987 colossus The Joshua Tree again and even reworking old songs for 2023’s Songs of Surrender, but nothing has uncorked the genie again, or given the band the kind of relevance they had for so many years. item.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
item.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. item.title: Beethoven: Symphony No 3 album review – thrilling, but Minasi’s determination to shock often feels self-conscious
item.description: Ensemble Resonanz/Minasi (Harmonia Mundi) Riccardo Minasi radically reassesses the Eroica, bringing its acerbic innovation to the fore in a startling and compelling new recording that will surely prompt heated debate In 1816, a young Franz Schubert took a swipe at Beethoven, accusing him of promoting a musical eccentricity that muddled “the agreeable with the repulsive, heroism with howlings and the holiest with harlequinades” in order to “goad people to madness”. In this colours-to-the-mast recording, Riccardo Minasi demonstrates precisely what contemporaries were afraid of with a radical reassessment of the Eroica Symphony. Looking to original sources, he strips away the modifications of centuries to lay the symphony before us in all its acerbic 19th-century innovation. The results are certainly startling. item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
